\textbf{Accuracy on instructed-lie benchmarks does not identify deception: the intervention that creates the lie also changes instruction-following behavior}---so its accuracy cannot be read as evidence of deception \textbf{as opposed to instruction-induced behavior}. \textbf{We do not ask whether LLMs can detect deception; we ask whether current benchmarks provide evidence that they do.} The reason is structural: \textbf{no experiment that intervenes only on the instruction can separate a detector response mediated by deception from one mediated by instruction-following}, both being descendants of that instruction. A deception-attribution reading needs $\tau_D$, which the identified $\tau_E$---the \emph{instruction}'s effect---neither bounds nor signs, so no gain in accuracy or scale resolves it. \textbf{This is an identification problem, not a generalization one: generalization can be perfect while identification fails.} \textbf{Our contribution is an operational identification audit for behavioral LLM benchmarks, together with empirical evidence that the common instructed-lie paradigm produces large, reproducible attribution failures across three detector paradigms, and that benchmark design can determine which behavioral signal appears to constitute ``deception detection''.} The audit has five parts: \textbf{one necessary construct-validity test no instructed design can supply}, three alternative-explanation diagnostics and one robustness test. Fixed elicitation itself is not new---trained belief-verified organisms have it---but not as the \emph{construct-validity criterion} for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy. Across three detector paradigms, equalizing the prompt \textbf{leaves no detectable above-chance discrimination on any of the six targets} (97.0\%$\to$\textbf{43.3\%}), and \textbf{the accuracy the benchmark is scored on is reachable with no learned features at all}: a parameter-free lexical rule reaches 69--80\%---\emph{surface-accessible accuracy}, not a decomposition of the detector's signal. Because \textbf{no public release we audited supplies all five}, we built materials that do: with deception operationalized independently of the detector's input, prior work's own battery separates operationally verified deception on three of five targets (two underpowered nulls), of which \textbf{a blinded re-run replicates two and a pre-registered covariate audit withdraws one, so the standing count is one of five}, with \textbf{one of five \emph{new} targets positive}. That is a demonstration that criterion-4-valid materials can produce a deception-associated signal, \textbf{not an estimate of the prevalence or reliability of deception detection}. \textbf{Read instructed-benchmark accuracy as evidence about the intervention, not about deception detection}: the canonical benchmark fails to identify deception, while a fixed-elicitation design reveals \emph{target-dependent} deception-associated signals---still not $\tau_D$---\textbf{rung~4 of five}. \textbf{Scope: English; open-weight models 3B--70B, plus seven frontier-scale targets from seven organizations; instructed-roleplay evaluations except where criterion~4 requires otherwise.}

\paragraph{Relation to prior work.} White-box probes read deception from activations~\citep{zou2023representation, burns2022discovering, azaria2023internal}; the black-box line's closest instance---our primary audit target---is \citet{pacchiardi2023catch}, and we audit both paradigms (§\ref{sec:td_vs_fd}). Three concurrent evaluations~\citep{kretschmar2025liarsbench, cooney2026didyoulie, hopkins2026liedetectors} find lie detectors fail to \textbf{generalize} beyond the regime they were fit in. That is a generalization question; ours is the prior one: instructed-lie accuracy is \textbf{not merely poorly generalizing but uninterpretable as evidence about deception}, because the intervention moves deception and compliance together---so generalization can be perfect while identification still fails. \textbf{Fixed elicitation is also not what we claim to introduce}---\citet{cooney2026didyoulie}'s trained organisms have it and go \emph{beyond} it, with $D$ \emph{set} rather than observed. \textbf{Our novelty is using it as the missing construct-validity criterion for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy}: we formalize the identification failure, turn it into an auditable protocol, and \textbf{show empirically that the confound accounts for substantial benchmark accuracy across three independent detector paradigms}---while auditing whether public artifacts supply the criterion at all. \paragraph{The Elicitation--Construct Confounding Principle (ECCP).} \emph{When a benchmark creates its target construct $Y$ by an intervention $E$ that also changes the elicited behavior $C$ a detector reads, no score evaluated only under $\mathrm{do}(E)$ is attributable to $Y$.} The Proposition below is that statement for $k$ unobserved mechanisms; \textbf{behavioral deception detection is the instantiation $(M_1,M_2)=(D,C)$}. \textbf{It also names an escape route a designer controls, and public corpora already take it piecewise}: of \textbf{28} pinned public corpora, \textbf{2, 21 and 3} supply each of the three properties that make a benchmark auditable on $Y$---crossing elicitation with items, recording the channel a detector reads, grading $Y$ off that channel---and \textbf{none supplies all three}, so an auditable benchmark needs no new idea, only the combination. \textbf{Outside deception the precondition is thus decidable and decided; the magnitude is measured only for deception} (EXP-AF, Appendix~\ref{app:eccp_decidability}).

\textbf{We establish:} \textbf{(1)}~instructed-roleplay designs identify the \emph{instruction}'s effect and cannot bound \emph{deception}'s---an \emph{identification} failure, not a detector failure; \textbf{(2)}~the confound is \emph{active}, not hypothetical, across \emph{three} detector paradigms, the score moving inside a single deception label; \textbf{(3)}~across \emph{both} public rollout releases, nine of ten rollout sets cannot express the criterion that removes the confound on a deployed-observable channel, and the closest fail three ways: an instrument-specific null, \textbf{annotation-channel leakage}, and \textbf{construct recovery}; and \textbf{(4)}~on materials we built to satisfy §1's (i)--(v), prior work's own battery \emph{does} separate operationally verified deception on three of five targets with power; a blinded re-run replicates two, plus one of five \emph{new} targets, and \textbf{a pre-registered covariate audit withdraws one, leaving one of five standing} (EXP-C4B/AE); and \textbf{(5)}~\textbf{the audit changes \emph{which} behavior indicates deception}---the instructed benchmark's best probe is inert at fixed $E$, another replacing it (EXP-AD). \textbf{The contribution is an operational identification audit for behavioral LLM benchmarks, together with empirical evidence that the common instructed-lie paradigm produces large, reproducible attribution failures across three detector paradigms and that benchmark design can determine which behavioral signal appears to constitute ``deception detection''.}

\emph{What would break it.} Negating (A4) with an observable that is a child of $D$ and of no other $M_i$---an exclusion restriction, i.e.\ an instrument; negating (A5) with a parametric assumption strong enough to allocate the effect, which then carries the attribution rather than the data; or negating (A2) with $\mathrm{do}(D)$, the top rung of Table~\ref{tab:criteria}, or with intervention~(B), $\mathrm{do}(E)$ at $D$ fixed (EXP-IB, §\ref{app:intervention_b}). \textbf{Criterion~4 negates (A3), not (A2)}: it makes $E$ degenerate and grades $D$ from a channel outside the detector's input, so $D$ becomes observed while remaining unmanipulated. That buys an association at fixed elicitation---rung~4---and not $\tau_D$, because a latent $U$ with $U\!\to\!D$ and $U\!\to\!S$ is untouched. \textbf{The algebra is standard; what this paper contributes is the protocol that enforces it on a published benchmark} (§\ref{app:related_work}).

The five criteria of §\ref{sec:eval_controls} are not interchangeable, and conflating them is how a benchmark comes to read a robustness result as an attribution result. \textbf{Only criterion~4 removes the elicitation confound}, and it is therefore necessary---though not sufficient---for an attribution to deception; the other four are supporting validity diagnostics, so failing one of them weakens the evidential basis for an attribution claim whereas failing criterion~4 forecloses attribution from the design itself. Criterion~4 as any published corpus can supply it is observational at fixed $E$: it establishes a deception-\emph{associated} signal, whereas identifying $\tau_D$ requires $D$ manipulated or randomized, the top rung of Table~\ref{tab:criteria}. \textbf{Three questions, and only the third is ours.} The generalization studies ask \emph{does the detector transfer}, and answer no; the belief-verified organisms ask \emph{can a valid contrast be built}, and answer yes, going \emph{beyond} criterion~4 with $D$ \textbf{set} rather than observed (Table~\ref{tab:criteria}'s last row). Neither asks \emph{whether the published accuracy licensed the deception reading in the first place}---and that is a different question in two ways that matter. \textbf{It is decidable from a design's specification}: requirements~(i)--(v) are properties of a design, so an auditor who never runs the detector can settle them, which is how we decide them on ten designs in five groups, four of them outside deception (Table~\ref{tab:prior_work_criteria}). \textbf{Decidable from a design, however, is not the same as decidable from what a release publishes}, and a pre-registered blinded panel says so: three rater families scoring all 18 audited cases from release-authored text alone, with no access to our verdicts, reproduce our~(i) reading wherever our packets are faithful (13/13) and overturn, by majority on all four, the sets whose published ``$E$ fixed'' flag is vacuous, but fall below the pre-registered $\alpha\!=\!0.40$ floor on every requirement ($\alpha\!=\!0.03$--$0.26$), with~(v) \textsc{undecidable} on 59\% of ratings (EXP-AA, Appendix~\ref{app:audit_agreement}). \textbf{We therefore narrow the claim rather than defend it}: (i)--(v) are decidable \emph{given} a specification at the resolution they require, and the releases audited here do not publish one---which is a sharper form of this paper's own complaint, and also a retraction of the stronger wording. And \textbf{it is invisible in the benchmark's output}: the reported accuracy is the same number whether or not the criterion holds, so no amount of transfer testing, scale, or held-out evaluation surfaces it---a design that fails~(i) and one that satisfies it are indistinguishable from their metrics. This is why a generalization result cannot substitute for the audit: a detector could transfer perfectly across every lie type in \citet{kretschmar2025liarsbench} and the instructed contrast would still not identify $\tau_D$.

The constraint itself is a standard non-identifiability result, whose premises we state in full (§\ref{app:criteria_taxonomy}); what is new is threefold, and worth separating from it. We \textbf{formalize} the identification failure for the instructed-lie paradigm; we \textbf{turn it into a protocol an auditor can apply to a benchmark they did not build}, which is what §\ref{sec:eval_controls}'s five criteria are for and what Table~\ref{tab:prior_work_criteria} exercises on ten designs; and we \textbf{show empirically that the confound accounts for substantial benchmark accuracy across three independent detector paradigms}---prior work's black-box battery, a hand-written surface rule and a white-box linear probe---rather than raising it as a possibility and setting it aside. The same holds on both public releases.
